Operation Weserübung: 1940 German invasion of Denmark and Norway in WWII.
Born to minor Prussian nobility, he commanded the Imperial German Army in WWI and, though no friend of Nazism, as German president handed Hitler the chancellorship in 1933 — who was he?
Paul von Hindenburg: President of Germany from 1925 to 1934.

Fought from 1919 to 1921, this conflict pitted the newly independent Second Republic under Józef Piłsudski against Lenin's forces seeking to spread revolution westward, redrawing Eastern Europe's borders after the collapse of the Central Powers. What conflict was this?
Polish–Soviet War: 20th-century conflict between Poland and Russia.
A New Brunswick lawyer who became one of the wealthiest Canadians of his era, he later took office as the country's 11th prime minister in 1930 — right as the Depression bit. Who was he?
R. B. Bennett: Prime Minister of Canada from 1930 to 1935.
Beginning 1 May 2019 when Naruhito ascended the Chrysanthemum Throne, this current chapter of Japan's imperial calendar takes its name from a phrase meaning 'beautiful harmony' — what is it called?
Reiwa era: Era of Japanese history (2019–present)
Prince Gustaf Adolf, Duke of Västerbotten
Roman Shukhevych: Ukrainian nationalist militant (1907–1950). Shukhevych led some of the Galicia-Volhynia massacres, where tens of thousands of Polish civilians were killed.
This twelve-year Central American conflict, fought between a U.S.-backed government and the FMLN guerrilla coalition, formally ended with the 1992 Chapultepec Peace Accords — which conflict?
Salvadoran Civil War: 1979–1992 conflict in El Salvador.
Ruling Korea's Joseon dynasty from 1418 to 1450, this monarch is remembered above all for creating Hangul, the native Korean alphabet — who was he?

Sejong the Great: King of Joseon from 1418 to 1450. Sejong (Korean: 세종; Hanja: 世宗; May 15, 1397 – April 8, 1450), commonly known as Sejong the Great (세종대왕; 世宗大王), was the fourth monarch of the Koreanic state Joseon.
Dubbed 'the father of modern Kazakh history and ethnography,' this 19th-century scholar took part in the Great Game and has Kazakhstan's national science academy named in his honor — who is he?
The 39th vice president of the United States, he resigned in 1973 under Nixon, becoming only the second VP in history to do so — who was he?
Spiro Agnew: Vice President of the United States from 1969 to 1973.
In 2007 this French politician became the first woman to reach the second round of a presidential election, ultimately losing to Nicolas Sarkozy — who is she?
Raised by his mother Aethra before discovering his royal father in Athens, this Greek hero is famed for slaying the Minotaur — who is he?
Theseus: Legendary king of Athens who slayed the Minotaur.
Founded by Mamata Banerjee in 1998 as a breakaway faction, this West Bengal party ruled from 2011 until finally losing to the BJP in the 2026 election — which party?
Trinamool Congress: Political party in India.
Born to a murdered Arvernian aristocrat, this Gallic chieftain united the tribes of Gaul in a doomed revolt against Julius Caesar's legions — who was he?
Sometimes anachronistically called Elizabeth, this woman was empress consort to China's last emperor before later becoming empress consort of the Japanese puppet state of Manchukuo — who was she?
Wanrong: Empress of Manchukuo from 1934 to 1945 (1906–1946)
Alongside Andrew Moray, this Scottish knight won the Battle of Stirling Bridge in 1297 before being captured and executed for treason in 1305 — who is he?
William Wallace: Scottish knight (1270–1305). Along with Andrew Moray, Wallace defeated an English army at the Battle of Stirling Bridge in September 1297.
October 1973: the holiest day of the Jewish calendar collided with the 10th day of Ramadan when Arab forces launched a surprise attack on Israel. What war broke out?
Yom Kippur War: 1973 war between Israel and Arab states.
Which one below was born first?
Henrietta Swan Leavitt (born 1868) is the earliest of the four. Henrietta Swan Leavitt (July 4, 1868 – December 12, 1921) was an American astronomer.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Anna Atkins (born 1799) is the earliest of the four. Anna Atkins (née Children; 16 March 1799 – 9 June 1871) was an English botanist and photographer.
Who among these four was born earliest?
Qian Xuesen (born 1911) is the earliest of the four. Qian received his undergraduate education in mechanical engineering at National Chiao Tung University in Shanghai in 1934.
COBOL (founded 1959) is the earliest of the four.
Who among these is an astronomer?
Mikhail Lomonosov is an astronomer. One of the founders of modern geology, Lomonosov was also a poet and influenced the formation of the modern Russian literary language.
Pick the mathematician from these four.
Gerardus Mercator is a mathematician. Gerardus Mercator (5 March 1512 – 2 December 1594) was a Flemish geographer, cosmographer and cartographer.
What is the atomic number of Zirconium?
Zirconium is a chemical element; it has symbol Zr and atomic number 40.
What is the atomic number of Francium?
Francium is a chemical element; it has symbol Fr and atomic number 87.
In what year was António de Oliveira Salazar born?
António de Oliveira Salazar: The regime he created lasted until 1974, making it one of the longest-lived authoritarian dictatorships in modern Europe.
In what year was Thomas Hobbes born?
Thomas Hobbes: Hobbes's academic journey began in Westport, leading him to the University of Oxford, where he was exposed to classical literature and mathematics.
In what year was Rosalind Franklin born?
Rosalind Franklin: Rosalind Elsie Franklin (25 July 1920 – 16 April 1958) was an English chemist and X-ray crystallographer.
In what year did Stephen Hawking die?
Stephen Hawking: Hawking was born in Oxford into a family of physicians.
In what year did John Money die?
John Money: Money researched paraphilia, including pedophilia, and pioneered the use of drug treatment to extinguish the libido of sex offenders.
In what year was Polyester discovered?
Polyester is a category of polymers that contain one or two ester linkages in every repeat unit of their main chain.
Information theory: Claude Shannon. Information theory is the mathematical study of the quantification, storage, and communication of a particular type of mathematically defined information.
Midazolam: Pfizer. It induces sleepiness, decreases anxiety, and causes anterograde amnesia.
Which country is Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil from?
Eurocopter AS350 Écureuil: France. The AS355 Ecureuil 2 is a twin-engine variant, marketed in North America as the TwinStar.
Who is credited with discovering Photography?
Who is credited with discovering Entropy?

 {\displaystyle \log }, the logarithm, varies for different applications.
Who is credited with discovering Scandium?
Scandium: Lars Fredrik Nilson. Scandium is a chemical element; it has symbol Sc and atomic number 21.
First added to the DSM in 1980 and diagnosed in women twice as often as men, this condition describes an intense, maladaptive reaction to a stressful life event — what is it?
Adjustment disorder is a mental disorder defined by a maladaptive response to a psychosocial stressor.
This cation forms when a proton attaches to ammonia, giving living organisms a vital source of nitrogen — what ion is it?
Ammonium is a modified form of ammonia that has an extra hydrogen atom.
Fill in the blank: “____ (April 21, 1971 - September 30, 2011) was an American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer.”

Anwar al-Awlaki (April 21, 1971 - September 30, 2011) was an American-Yemeni Islamic cleric and lecturer. Al-Awlaki was the first U.S. citizen to be targeted and assassinated by a U.S. government drone strike.
Part of the family Ericaceae, these shrubs flower in April and May in the Northern Hemisphere and October and November south of the equator — what are they called?
Azalea (-) are flowering shrubs in the genus Rhododendron, particularly the former subgenera Tsutsusi (evergreen) and Pentanthera (deciduous).
This red-orange compound, formed from the breakdown of heme, is further processed into pigments that give feces their brown color and urine its straw-yellow hue. What is it?
Bilirubin (BR) (adopted from German, originally bili, for bile, plus ruber, Latin for red) is a red-orange compound that occurs as the reduction product of biliverdin, a breakdown product of heme.
This flowering plant family is known for flowers with four petals arranged in a cross shape, and includes crops ranging from leafy greens to root vegetables to condiment seeds. Name the family?
Brassicaceae (the older but equally valid) Cruciferae is a medium-sized and economically important family of flowering plants commonly known as the mustards, the crucifers, or the cabbage family.

Standing in contrast to the 'cat-like' carnivorans that diversified across Africa and southern Asia, this suborder unites dogs, bears, raccoons, and pinnipeds under one 'dog-like' umbrella — what's it called?
Caniformia is a suborder within the order Carnivora consisting of "dog-like" carnivorans.

Appointed royal executioner under Louis XVI and later chief executioner of the First Republic, this Frenchman personally carried out the executions of the king, his queen, and Robespierre — who is he?
Charles-Henri Sanson (French; 15 February 1739 - 4 July 1806), was the royal executioner of France during the reign of King Louis XVI, and later chief executioner of the First French Republic.

Largely self-taught and grinding his own lenses from spare parts on a Kansas farm, this astronomer's homemade skills landed him at Lowell Observatory — where his 1930 survey turned up the first known body in the Kuiper belt; who was he?

Clyde Tombaugh (February 4, 1906 - January 17, 1997) was an American astronomer and telescope maker, best known for discovering Pluto in 1930, marking the first detection of what would eventually be recognized as the Kuiper belt.
Native to Europe and Western Asia, this birch-family shrub produces the round nuts sold commercially as hazelnuts — which species?
Corylus avellana is a species of flowering plant in the birch family Betulaceae.
Often called eczema, this umbrella term covers skin inflammation marked by itchiness, redness, and a rash, sometimes with small blisters or thickened skin — what is it?
Dermatitis is a term used for different types of skin inflammation, typically characterized by itchiness, redness and a rash.
Sometimes triggered by lead poisoning or reactions to neuroleptic drugs, this neurological disorder produces involuntary, twisting muscle contractions — what is it?

Dystonia is a neurological hyperkinetic movement disorder in which sustained or repetitive muscle contractions occur involuntarily, resulting in twisting and repetitive movements or abnormal fixed postures.
Also known as human herpesvirus 4, this common virus was the first identified oncogenic virus and causes infectious mononucleosis in 90% of cases. What is it?
Epstein–Barr virus (EBV), also known as human herpesvirus 4 (HHV-4), is one of the nine known human herpesvirus types in the herpes family, and is one of the most common viruses in humans.
This intracellular protein buffers the body against both iron deficiency and iron overload, and small amounts leak into the blood where doctors measure it as a diagnostic marker — what protein is it?
Ferritin is a universal intracellular and extracellular protein that stores iron and releases it in a controlled fashion.

This genus of scented flowering shrubs in the coffee family was named for an 18th-century naturalist, though Carl Linnaeus gets most of the credit over the botanist who first proposed it — which genus?
Gardenia is a genus of flowering plants in the coffee family, Rubiaceae, native to the tropical and subtropical regions of Africa, Asia, Madagascar, Pacific Islands, and Australia.

This American computer scientist and Navy rear admiral devised the theory of machine-independent programming languages and used it to help create COBOL, after being one of the first programmers on the Harvard Mark I — who is she?
Grace Hopper (ne Murray; December 9, 1906 - January 1, 1992) was an American computer scientist, mathematician, and United States Navy rear admiral.

Producer of Japan's first major turn-based role-playing video game, this Dutch-born American entrepreneur also secured console distribution rights to a Russian puzzle game and resolved the licensing disputes that brought it to the Game Boy — who is he?
Henk Rogers is a Dutch-born American video game designer and entrepreneur.

This large insect order includes sawflies, wasps, bees, and ants, with more than 150,000 described species, many of whose females have an egg-laying organ often modified into a stinger — what is it called?
Hymenoptera is a large order of insects, comprising the sawflies, wasps, bees, and ants.

Also known by the old names green vitriol and copperas, this heptahydrate salt dissolves in water to form a paramagnetic, octahedral aquo complex and is used medically to fight anemia — which compound is it?
Iron(II) sulfate (British) denotes a range of salts with the formula FeSO4xH2O.

He wrote the first commercial anti-virus software in 1987 and ran twice for the Libertarian presidential nomination — yet later urged people to uninstall the very product that still bears his name. Who is he?
John McAfee (18 September 1945 - 23 June 2021) was a British and American computer programmer, businessman, and two-time U.S.
Built from four fused rings, compounds in this class include cholesterol, testosterone, and anti-inflammatory drugs like dexamethasone. What class of compound is it?
Kurt Gödel (April 28, 1906 - January 14, 1978) was a logician, mathematician, cosmologist, and philosopher.
One of only five people to win multiple Nobel Prizes, this American chemist and peace activist is the sole person to have received two unshared Nobels — one in Chemistry, one for Peace. Who is he?
Linus Pauling (February 28, 1901 - August 19, 1994) was an American chemist and peace activist.

This colorless, highly water-soluble inorganic salt forms hydrates holding up to 12 water molecules per unit, and its anhydrous form is industry's main source for producing a lightweight, silvery-white structural metal — which compound is it?
Magnesium chloride is an inorganic compound with the formula MgCl2.
First isolated from a cow's pineal gland in 1958 because it could lighten the skin of frogs, this nighttime hormone went on to become famous for governing the sleep-wake cycle — what is it?
Melatonin is a natural compound produced by various organisms, including bacteria and eukaryotes.
This SI base unit for amount of substance, symbol mol, is defined so that one unit contains exactly 6.02214076×10²³ elementary entities — what is it called?
Mole (unit) (symbol mol) is a unit of measurement, the base unit in the International System of Units (SI) for amount of substance.

Which form of alternative medicine, rooted in vitalism and folk healing rather than evidence, gathers 'natural' and 'self-healing' practices ranging from discredited homeopathy to accepted psychotherapy?
Naturopathy is a form of alternative medicine. The ethics of naturopathy have been called into question by medical professionals and its practice has been characterized as quackery.
This massive bony fish, weighing up to a metric ton, resembles a giant fish head without a tail and is native to tropical and temperate waters worldwide. What is it?
Ocean sunfish (Mola mola), also known as the common mola, is one of the largest bony fish in the world.
Pair it with aspirin and caffeine and it's a first-line remedy for mild headaches; on its own it's the active ingredient many people know as acetaminophen — what is this over-the-counter drug?
Paracetamol is an analgesic and antipyretic agent used to treat fever and mild to moderate pain.

Fill in the blank: “____ (PD) is a benign, acquired penile connective tissue disease characterized by the occurrence of fibrotic plaques within the tunica albuginea - the dense elastic covering of the corpora cavernosa.”

Peyronie's disease (PD) is a benign, acquired penile connective tissue disease characterized by the occurrence of fibrotic plaques within the tunica albuginea - the dense elastic covering of the corpora cavernosa. The plaques cause abnormal curvature, pain, penile deformities (e.g., narrowing or indentation), and usually erectile dysfunction, particularly during erection.

This genus of fragrant flowering shrubs, native to Mexico, Central America, and the Caribbean, is widely grown as an ornamental in Hawaii and in desert climates of the Arabian Peninsula — name the genus?
Plumeria is a genus of flowering plants in the family Apocynaceae.
A single long chain of amino acids is called a polypeptide — string enough of them together and you get this folded macromolecule whose 3D shape determines what job it does. What is it?
Protein are large biomolecules and macromolecules that comprise one or more long chains of amino acid residues.

This bird of prey now breeds only in Europe, though it once also ranged across West Asia and Northwest Africa, with northern populations historically wintering as far as western Africa — what bird is it?
Red kite (Milvus milvus) is a bird of prey in the family Accipitridae, which also includes many other diurnal raptors such as eagles, buzzards, and harriers.
This root vegetable — a hybrid of cabbage and a related turnip-like plant — goes by different names in North America and Britain, and is often confused for a big turnip. What is it?
Rutabaga (North American English) or swede (British English and some Commonwealth English) is a root vegetable, a form of Brassica napus (which also includes rapeseed).

This potentially life-threatening condition occurs when the body's dysregulated response to infection damages its own tissues and organs, often causing fever, rapid heartbeat, and confusion — what is it called?
Sepsis is a potentially life-threatening condition that arises when the body's dysregulated response to infection causes injury to its own tissues and organs.
Found throughout the nightshade family — including in potato leaves, fruit, and tubers — this saponin-family toxin doubles as the plant's own natural pesticide. What compound is it?
Solanine is a glycoalkaloid poison found in species of the nightshade family within the genus Solanum, such as the potato (Solanum tuberosum).
In the equation 5 − 2 = 3, this is the operation being performed — which one is it?
Subtraction (which is signified by the minus sign) is one of the four arithmetic operations along with addition, multiplication and division.
Caused by Clostridium tetani, this infection brings on recurring muscle spasms that can last weeks and prove fatal in about 10% of cases — what is it commonly known as?
Tetanus (from Ancient Greek 'tension', 'stretched', 'rigid'), also known as lockjaw, is a bacterial infection caused by Clostridium tetani and characterized by muscle spasms.
Roughly eight times more potent than an older analogue, this bleeding-control medication is also prescribed for hereditary angioedema — what is it?
Tranexamic acid is a medication used to treat or prevent excessive blood loss from major trauma, postpartum bleeding, surgery, tooth removal, nosebleeds, and heavy menstruation.
This type of blood vessel usually carries deoxygenated blood toward the heart — except in the pulmonary and fetal circulation, where it carries oxygen-rich blood instead — what is it?
Vein is a blood vessel in the circulatory system of humans and most other animals that carries blood towards the heart.
This broad category of limbless, tube-bodied animals ranges from microscopic creatures to a marine species measured at nearly 58 meters long — the longest animal on Earth — what are they called?
Worm are many different distantly related bilateral animals that typically have a long cylindrical tube-like body, no limbs, and usually no eyes.

This organic compound functions as a neurotransmitter in the brain and body of many animal types, including humans. It is the chemical that motor neurons release at the neuromuscular junction to enable muscle movement. What is it?
Acetylcholine: Organic chemical and neurotransmitter. Its name is derived from its chemical structure: it is an ester of acetic acid and choline.
Born in 1929 and died in 2001, this man was a respected Saudi Islamic scholar — who is he?
This Indian economist and philosopher won the 1998 Nobel Prize in Economic Sciences for his work on welfare economics, and later received India's highest civilian honor — who is he?
Amartya Sen: Indian economist and Nobel laureate (born 1933)
Named by paleontologist Barnum Brown in 1908, this armored dinosaur is considered the archetypal member of its group despite no complete skeleton ever being found — which genus?
Ankylosaurus: Ankylosaurid dinosaur genus from the Late Cretaceous Period.
Also called gobō, this Eurasian plant is cultivated in Japan for its edible root but has become an invasive weed of high-nitrogen soils elsewhere — which species?
Arctium lappa: Species of flowering plant. It has become an invasive weed of high-nitrogen soils in North America, Australia, and other regions, but is cultivated for its vegetable root.
This British mathematician and logician coined the phrase 'mathematical induction' and gave his name to a pair of laws relating conjunction, disjunction, and negation. Who was he?
Augustus De Morgan: British mathematician and logician (1806–1871)
In continuous production since 1974 — the longest run of any civilian turboprop plane in its class — this twin-engine model also serves in medevac and flight-inspection roles — what is it?
Beechcraft Super King Air: Light twin-turboprop transport aircraft family.
Not a species of its own, it's really a melanistic leopard or jaguar whose rosettes are still hidden under the dark coat — what do we call this big-cat colour variant?
Black panther: Variant of leopard and jaguar. Black panthers of both species have excess black pigments, but their typical rosettes are also present.
This subfamily of horned, cloven-hooved ungulates includes cattle, bison, and both African and water buffalo, with the gaur as its largest living member — which group?
In 1930, which Indian physicist won the Nobel Prize for discovering that light changes wavelength when passing through a transparent material, becoming the first Asian to win a Physics Nobel?

Defined by a –COOH functional group attached to an R-group, and only partially dissociating in water, this general class of organic compounds includes fatty compounds and the building blocks of proteins — what is this functional class called?
Carboxylic acid: Organic compound containing a –C(=O)OH group.
Often called the Judas tree, this small deciduous redbud native to Southern Europe and Western Asia bursts into deep pink blossoms each spring — what species is it?

Caused by a bacterium spread through contaminated water and undercooked shellfish, this intestinal infection produces severe watery diarrhea that can trigger dehydration within hours — which disease is it?
Cholera: Bacterial infection of the small intestine.
Commonly called the tailbone, this bone is the vestigial remnant of a tail in humans and other tailless primates, sitting just below the sacrum — which bone?
Coccyx: Bone of the pelvis. In tailless primates (e.g. humans and other great apes) since Nacholapithecus (a Miocene hominoid), the coccyx is the remnant of a vestigial tail.
One of the few metals found in nature in directly usable metallic form, this soft, pinkish-orange element with symbol Cu prizes its high thermal and electrical conductivity — what is it?
Copper: Chemical element with atomic number 29 (Cu)
Caused by prolonged exposure to excess cortisol, this condition produces abdominal weight gain with thin limbs, a rounded red face, and reddish stretch marks — which condition is it?
Cushing's syndrome: Symptoms from excessive exposure to glucocorticoids such as cortisol.

Known mainly through DNA evidence rather than plentiful fossils, this extinct archaic human group ranged across Asia until about 32,000 years ago, and DNA analysis confirmed the Harbin skull belonged to it — what group is it?
Denisovan: Archaic human species from Asia.
In 1949, this NASA mathematician became the first African-American woman to supervise a team at Langley, later teaching herself and her staff the Fortran language — who is she?
Dorothy Vaughan: American human computer and computer programmer (1910–2008)
This group of 13 genetic connective tissue disorders causes loose joints and stretchy, velvety skin, with a classification last updated in 2017 — what condition is it?
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome: Group of genetic connective tissues disorders. The existing classification was last updated in 2017, when a number of rarer forms of EDS were added.
Despite never earning a university degree, this German-American psychoanalyst taught at Harvard, Berkeley, and Yale, and coined the term 'identity crisis' — who is he?
Erik Erikson: American psychoanalyst and essayist (1902–1994)

With a red face, a black-and-white head, and a bold yellow wing bar, this small finch native to the Palearctic often appears in Italian Renaissance paintings of the Madonna and Child. What bird is it?
European goldfinch: Species of bird. It has been introduced to other areas, including Australia, New Zealand, Uruguay and the United States.
Once tapped as a source of natural rubber, though no longer used commercially for that purpose, this houseplant native to South and Southeast Asia is nicknamed the 'rubber tree.' Which species?
Ficus elastica: Species of banyan tree.
Working in Feynman's group on the Manhattan Project before co-detecting an elusive elementary particle with Clyde Cowan, he won the 1995 Nobel for catching the neutrino — who was he?
Deriving its name from Greek words for 'earth' and 'study of', this branch of natural science examines rocks and the processes that have shaped the planet over time — what is it called?
Geology: Scientific study of Earth's physical composition.
This Intel co-founder proposed the famous observation that the number of transistors on a chip roughly doubles every two years — who is he?
This inherited disorder leaves blood unable to clot properly, causing prolonged bleeding after injury and, in its two main forms, low levels of clotting factor VIII or IX — which condition?
Haemophilia: Genetic disease involving blood clotting.
Spread mainly through blood-to-blood contact, this viral infection becomes chronic in about 70 percent of those first infected and can lead to liver failure over decades — which disease?
Hepatitis C: Human viral infection. Hepatitis C is an infectious disease caused by the hepatitis C virus (HCV) that primarily affects the liver; it is a type of viral hepatitis.

This field, drawing on sociology, anthropology, economics, and environmental science, studies how communities interact with their habitats — from urban sprawl to cultural and economic patterns across space — which discipline?
Human geography: Study of cultures, communities, people, lifestyle, and activities of people of the world.

Named from the Greek word for "fish" because of its dry, scaly skin, this family of genetic skin disorders ranges from a mild type mistaken for ordinary dry skin to a rare, life-threatening form — which condition?
Ichthyosis: Family of disorders causing dry, thickened, scaly skin.

Native to the Americas but now grown worldwide, one species of this flowering plant genus has become such a popular ornamental that it's classified as an invasive weed on four continents — which genus?
Jacaranda: Genus of trees. The generic name is also used as the common name.

The id Software programmer behind Wolfenstein 3D, Doom, and Quake later left to become CTO of Oculus VR — before walking away again to chase artificial general intelligence. Which 3D-graphics wizard is he?
John Carmack: American computer programmer and video game developer (born 1970)
Marketed as Nizoral, this antifungal medication also treats Cushing's syndrome and excess hair growth in women, though oral use risks liver damage — which drug?
Native to the Mediterranean and used to season food as a bay leaf, this aromatic evergreen prominent in classical Greco-Roman culture can grow up to 20 metres tall — what is its scientific name?
Laurus nobilis: Species of flowering plant in the laurel family Lauraceae.
Nearly always affecting women, this incurable condition causes fat buildup in both legs that's resistant to typical weight loss and often mistaken for other circulatory disorders — what is it?
Lipedema: Condition involving excessive deposition of fat in the legs.
The sole member of its genus in the soapberry family, this sweet, mildly tart fruit carries a distinctive rose-like aroma and comes in Indochinese, Philippine, and Javanese subspecies — what is it?

Often making people tall and thin with long fingers and very flexible joints, this connective-tissue disorder carries serious risks to the heart and aorta — caused by a mutation in the FBN1 fibrillin gene — which condition?
Marfan syndrome: Genetic disorder involving connective tissue.
Nicknamed a 'semi-lunar' cartilage for its half-moon shape, this crescent-shaped structure cushions joints like the knee, wrist, and jaw — what is it?
Meniscus (anatomy): Fibrocartilaginous part of a bone joint.

NATO called it 'Farmer,' and this Soviet twin-engine fighter was the first Soviet production aircraft capable of supersonic speed in level flight, later battling American jets over North Vietnam — which aircraft?
Mikoyan-Gurevich MiG-19: Air superiority fighter aircraft family.
Native to northern India, this fast-growing, drought-resistant tree is nicknamed the 'drumstick tree' for its seed pods and the 'horseradish tree' for its pungent roots — what is it?
Moringa oleifera: Species of flowering tree.
Sold as Aleve, this NSAID eases pain, fever, and menstrual cramps for up to twelve hours, and also comes in a more soluble sodium form — which drug?
Naproxen: Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drug (NSAID) used to treat pain.
Unlike its more predictably spreading cousin, this group of blood cancers can appear in multiple parts of the body at once and cause enlarged lymph nodes, fevers, and night sweats — which condition?
Non-Hodgkin lymphoma: Type of cancer of lymph nodes.
In this learning process, voluntary behaviors are shaped by their consequences — strengthened by reinforcement, weakened by punishment or extinction. What is it called?
Operant conditioning: Type of associative learning process for behavioral modification.
This B vitamin's name comes from the Greek for "from everywhere," since it turns up in nearly all foods, and animals need it to build coenzyme A — what is it?
A hybrid cross of watermint and spearmint, this herb is one of the oldest used in cooking and medicine and a key plant source of menthol — what is it?
Peppermint: Hybrid flowering plant in the family Lamiaceae.
Enclosed in a papery husk derived from its calyx, this nightshade genus includes the tomatillo and Cape gooseberry among its edible-fruited species — which genus?
Most commonly referring to a type called PET, this category of polymers built from ester linkages is often blended with cotton to reduce wrinkling — what is it called?
Polyester: Category of polymers, in which the monomers are joined together by ester links.
This Old World tree species has two main cultivar groups, the dark-red Morello and the lighter Amarelle, prized for their tart, edible pulp — which fruit-bearing plant?
Prunus cerasus: Species of cherry tree. Prunus cerasus (sour cherry, tart cherry, or dwarf cherry) is an Old World species of Prunus in the subgenus Cerasus (cherries).
A small herbivore of the family Leporidae and a cousin to hares, this prey animal has been introduced to every continent except Antarctica — what is it?
Rabbit: Mammals of the family Leporidae. The most widespread rabbit genera are Oryctolagus and Sylvilagus.
Responsible for at least half of all common colds, this tiny RNA virus in the Picornaviridae family measures only about 30 nanometers across — what is it?
Discovered in 1844 by Karl Ernst Claus and named in honor of Russia, which unreactive platinum-group element with atomic number 44 now caps extreme ultraviolet photomasks for chip lithography?
Ruthenium: Chemical element with atomic number 44 (Ru)
Exceeding 30 centimeters in length, this centipede from South America is the largest of its kind, preying on animals as large as small mammals and reptiles — which species?

Scolopendra gigantea: Species of Chilopoda (centipede). Scolopendra gigantea, also known as the Peruvian giant yellow-leg centipede or Amazonian giant centipede, is a centipede in the genus Scolopendra.

This medical condition of inadequate blood flow to body tissues comes in four flavors — hypovolemic, cardiogenic, obstructive, and distributive — and can progress to confusion or cardiac arrest if untreated — what is it called?
Shock (circulatory): Medical condition of insufficient blood flow. Shock is the state of insufficient blood flow to the tissues of the body as a result of problems with the circulatory system.

Self-taught from her father's library and writing to Gauss and Lagrange under a male pseudonym, this French mathematician pioneered elasticity theory and laid groundwork for Fermat's Last Theorem — who was she?
Sophie Germain: French mathematician, physicist, and philosopher.
